passages.title: The library beyond the shelves
passages.text:
A public library is sometimes defended as a storehouse of books, as though its value could be measured by the number of volumes on its shelves. That picture is incomplete. A library is also a place where people may spend time without being expected to buy anything, where a student can find a quiet desk, where a job seeker can use a computer, and where a child may encounter a story that no one at home has recommended. Its civic function lies partly in the fact that these activities occur side by side. A person who arrives for internet access may leave with a book; someone who attends a local history talk may discover a neighbour with whom to organise a neighbourhood project.

This does not mean that every branch must provide every service. A small library with a limited budget may need to choose between longer opening hours, new books, accessible equipment and community programmes. Decisions should be based on local needs rather than on an abstract belief that one model fits every place. A branch near a school may be used heavily after classes, while one in an area with many older residents may need stronger large-print and digital assistance services. Uniform standards can protect a minimum level of access, but sensible variation can make the service more useful.

Digital collections have widened the reach of libraries. A reader can borrow an electronic book from home, search catalogues across institutions and access material that a local branch could never store physically. Yet digital delivery does not remove the need for buildings. Devices fail, connections are uneven, and some users need help navigating a form or evaluating a source. A library worker can explain why a website is unreliable in a way that a search box cannot. A shared room also offers a form of social infrastructure: people can be present together without having to be customers, employees or guests of a private organisation.

The case for libraries should therefore avoid nostalgia. Their task is not simply to preserve an older technology. It is to maintain an open civic resource while adapting to changes in how information is created and used. Success should be assessed through more than loans or footfall. Useful measures include who can enter, whether the services meet local needs, whether information is accessible, and whether visitors gain the confidence to learn independently. A quiet building may be doing important work even when its most valuable outcome is not recorded in a circulation database.

passages.title: Living with urban heat
passages.text:
Heat in a city is not distributed evenly. A neighbourhood with mature trees, shaded pavements and buildings designed for ventilation may remain more comfortable than a nearby district dominated by dark roofs, wide roads and exposed concrete. The difference is not merely a matter of taste. High temperatures affect health, the ability to work, school attendance and the cost of cooling homes. They also reveal how planning decisions made over decades shape present-day risk.

A common response is to issue warnings during a heatwave. Such alerts are necessary, particularly for outdoor workers, older people, infants and those with existing health vulnerabilities. But an alert is not a substitute for reducing exposure. A resident who must cross a sunlit road to reach a bus stop cannot make the journey safer by reading a message on a phone. A street vendor may understand the danger and still lose income by stopping work. Public policy therefore needs both immediate protection and longer-term changes to the built environment.

Trees are often presented as a simple solution. They can provide shade, cool the air through evapotranspiration and make walking more pleasant. Yet planting a tree is not the same as creating a durable canopy. Species must suit local conditions, roots need room, water must be available during establishment, and someone must maintain the site. A programme that counts saplings planted but ignores survival rates can look successful in a report while producing little shade on the street. The same caution applies to reflective roofs, cool pavements and public drinking-water points: installation figures are inputs, not proof of benefits.

Heat planning also raises questions of fairness. Wealthier households may afford air-conditioning, insulation and flexible work arrangements. Poorer households may occupy crowded rooms, work outdoors or pay a larger share of income for electricity. Measures that reduce average city temperatures may still leave the most exposed residents with little relief. Mapping local heat, consulting communities and directing investment towards places with the highest combined exposure and limited capacity to adapt can make interventions more effective.

The purpose of a heat plan is not to promise that a city can eliminate hot weather. It is to reduce avoidable harm and make public space usable during increasingly difficult conditions. That requires reliable data, maintenance budgets and coordination between health agencies, transport authorities, housing departments and local governments. A warning system tells people that danger is approaching; thoughtful design changes how much danger they face when it arrives.

passages.title: Translation as an act of interpretation
passages.text:
Translation is often described as the transfer of words from one language to another. The description suggests a mechanical operation: find an equivalent term, replace the original and preserve the meaning. Anyone who has tried to translate a poem, a joke or a legal expression knows that the process is less orderly. Words carry histories, social relationships and associations that do not travel neatly across linguistic boundaries. A phrase that sounds affectionate in one language may seem formal or even dismissive in another.

A careful translator does not simply ask what a sentence says. The translator must also ask what it does. Is a speaker being ironic, respectful, evasive or threatening? Does a repeated word create rhythm, insistence or humour? Is a silence meaningful because the characters share a cultural assumption? These questions may require a translator to depart from the structure of the source sentence in order to preserve its effect. Literal fidelity can sometimes become a form of distortion if it produces a sentence that a reader would misunderstand.

The opposite danger is equally real. A translator who takes too many liberties may replace the author's world with the translator's preferences. An unfamiliar custom can be softened until it loses its distinctiveness; a politically difficult statement can be made more comfortable; a character's awkward speech can be polished into a voice that the original did not contain. Good translation therefore involves judgement bounded by responsibility. The translator must make choices, but those choices should be explainable by the text and its context rather than by a desire to improve it.

Readers also have a role. A translation is not a transparent window through which the original appears unchanged. It is a carefully constructed route into another work. Notes, introductions and parallel editions can help readers recognise where a word has no exact equivalent or where a historical reference carries several layers. Such aids should illuminate rather than overwhelm the work. Too much explanation can turn reading into a museum tour; too little can leave a reader mistaking a local convention for a universal one.

Translation is consequently both an intellectual craft and a public service. It allows ideas to circulate beyond the language community in which they first appeared, but it also shapes how those ideas are received. The best translator is neither an invisible machine nor a second author free to rewrite everything. The translator is an accountable interpreter who makes a work accessible while preserving enough of its strangeness to remind readers that another language may organise experience differently.

passages.title: What scientific uncertainty can and cannot tell us
passages.text:
Public debate often treats uncertainty as evidence that scientists do not know anything useful. When estimates of a risk change, critics may accuse researchers of inconsistency. Yet uncertainty is not always a weakness in scientific reasoning. It can be a precise description of what is known, what remains unknown and how strongly the available evidence supports a conclusion. A weather forecast that gives a probability of rain is not less scientific than one that offers a confident yes or no. It is more honest about the limits of prediction.

Scientific conclusions are also provisional in a disciplined sense. They may be revised when better measurements, larger samples or new methods become available. Revision does not mean that every earlier conclusion was careless. A medical recommendation based on a small trial may appropriately change after several larger studies. The relevant question is whether the change follows from stronger evidence and whether the earlier level of confidence was communicated accurately. A system that never revises its claims may be protecting its reputation rather than pursuing knowledge.

The public, however, needs more than a list of caveats. A statement that says evidence is uncertain without explaining the practical range of possible outcomes can be difficult to use. Researchers and public institutions should distinguish between uncertainty about the exact size of an effect and uncertainty about its direction. If evidence strongly indicates that a practice increases risk but cannot yet quantify the increase precisely, waiting for a perfect estimate may be unreasonable. Conversely, a small association observed in one study should not automatically justify a sweeping rule.

Institutions can improve communication by stating assumptions, identifying the quality of evidence, explaining what would cause a conclusion to change and separating scientific findings from policy choices. Science may estimate the consequences of several options, but deciding which risk society should accept also involves values such as fairness, liberty and cost. Those values should not be disguised as laboratory results. Nor should political disagreement be presented as though it automatically invalidates empirical work.

Uncertainty is useful when it guides better questions and more careful decisions. It becomes a problem when it is used selectively: demanding impossible certainty from evidence one dislikes while accepting weak support for a preferred claim. A mature public conversation can hold two ideas together. Knowledge may be incomplete, and action may still be necessary. The task is to match the confidence of a decision to the strength of the evidence, make the remaining uncertainty visible and remain willing to revise the decision when justified.

passages.title: The Union Budget and the language of priorities

sources.title: Union Budget 2026-27 Speech
sources.publisher: Ministry of Finance, Government of India

passages.text:
A Union Budget is both a financial statement and an account of the government's priorities. It sets out expected receipts and expenditure for a financial year, explains the policy direction of the executive and gives Parliament an opportunity to scrutinise how public money is proposed to be raised and spent. It is therefore misleading to treat the Budget as a list of announcements alone. A proposal may require legislation, delegated rules or administrative action before it changes what a citizen or business actually experiences.

The Union Budget for 2026–27 was presented on 1 February 2026 by Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman. The official summary described the Budget through three Kartavya priorities. The first was to accelerate and sustain economic growth. The second concerned fulfilling people's aspirations and building their capacity. The third was framed in the language of Sabka Sath, Sabka Vikas. The government also described the Budget as the first prepared in Kartavya Bhawan. Such framing matters politically because it explains how the executive wants the measures to be understood, but the framing itself does not reveal whether the measures will achieve their stated aims.

Among the announced measures was the commencement of the Income-tax Act, 2025 from April 2026, alongside a promise of simplified rules and forms. The summary also referred to changes for information-technology services, including a common safe-harbour margin and a higher threshold for access to that framework. Other announcements concerned customs treatment of selected capital goods, critical minerals and lithium-ion battery manufacturing, as well as securities transaction tax on futures. Each proposal has a different route from announcement to implementation. A tax statute, a notification and a customs exemption do not necessarily operate in the same way or on the same date.

A budget must also be evaluated against trade-offs. Lowering a tax or customs barrier may support investment or reduce the cost of production, but it can affect revenue. Public investment can improve infrastructure and productive capacity, yet projects need preparation and oversight to translate allocations into completed assets. A new rule may simplify compliance for one group while requiring transition work from another. It is therefore useful to distinguish the amount allocated, the legal authority for spending, the money actually released and the outcome ultimately achieved.

For a citizen reading a budget summary, the central questions are practical: who is affected, what legal or administrative step is still required, when does the change begin, and how will its results be measured? The Budget is an important starting point in the policy cycle, not the final evidence that a policy has succeeded.

passages.title: Courts, lawyers and fabricated legal authorities

sources.title: Landmark Judgment Summaries: Pooja Ramesh Singh v Jammu and Kashmir Bank Ltd, 2026 INSC 668

passages.text:
Generative artificial-intelligence systems can produce fluent answers that look authoritative while containing fabricated cases, quotations or citations. In a legal setting, that risk is especially serious. A court may rely on precedent to explain why a rule applies, distinguish an earlier decision or identify the limits of its own power. A citation that appears genuine but does not exist can distort that process. The problem is not that lawyers have begun using digital tools; it is that a polished output may be mistaken for a verified legal source.

In Pooja Ramesh Singh v Jammu and Kashmir Bank Ltd, decided on 2 July 2026 and identified as 2026 INSC 668, the Supreme Court addressed the use of AI-generated false or hallucinated legal citations in decisions of tribunals. The official summary describes a matter in which six AI-generated citations were later found to be nonexistent or to contain paragraphs that did not exist in the attributed decisions. The case arose in the context of insolvency proceedings involving a corporate debtor and a corporate guarantor. The central concern was the integrity of adjudication when a decision relies on material that cannot be authenticated.

A legal citation performs more than a decorative function. It allows another lawyer, litigant or judge to inspect the authority being invoked. Verification is therefore part of legal reasoning, not a clerical task that can safely be delegated to an automated system. A researcher may use software to locate possible authorities, compare documents or organise a large set of decisions. But the final responsibility to check whether a case exists, whether the quoted passage appears in it and whether the authority remains good law belongs to the person relying on it.

The issue also requires a distinction between a tool and its user. The mere fact that a researcher used an AI system does not establish that every statement produced is false. Equally, the fact that a citation looks plausible does not establish that it is authentic. The correct response is a verification process: locate the judgment in an official or trusted database, check the exact paragraph, confirm the court and date, and read enough of the decision to understand its context. If an authority cannot be located, it should not be presented as precedent.

The wider lesson extends beyond courts. Public institutions increasingly receive documents drafted with automated assistance, and they need processes that test sources rather than reward confident presentation. Technology can reduce the time needed to search, but it cannot remove the obligation to substantiate a claim. In adjudication, where reasons must be open to scrutiny, traceability is a condition of legitimacy.

passages.title: Electoral rolls and constitutional supervision

sources.title: Landmark Judgment Summaries: Association for Democratic Reforms v Election Commission of India, 2026 INSC 564

passages.text:
An electoral roll is the practical record through which eligible citizens are identified for voting in a constituency. Its accuracy matters in two directions. An eligible voter should not be wrongly excluded, while a person who is not entitled to be enrolled should not remain on the list. Errors may arise when people migrate, deaths are not reported, names are duplicated or records are not updated. A revision exercise is therefore an ordinary part of maintaining an electoral system, but its design can have serious consequences for individual participation.

In Association for Democratic Reforms v Election Commission of India, identified as 2026 INSC 564 and decided on 27 May 2026, the Supreme Court considered the legality of a Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls in Bihar. The official summary records questions about the Election Commission's constitutional authority, the Representation of the People Act, 1950, procedural rules, legitimate purpose and proportionality. It explains that the Commission's powers under Article 324 of the Constitution must be read alongside Parliament's legislative authority under Article 327. These provisions are complementary rather than competing: the Commission has constitutional responsibilities, but it must exercise them consistently with valid law.

The Court's summary also discusses Section 21(3) of the 1950 Act as a statutory source of power for directing a special revision. It records the Commission's stated concerns, including demographic change, large-scale migration, duplicate entries and its responsibility to support accurate electoral rolls. The Court examined whether the chosen measures had a rational connection with the stated objectives and whether the exercise was excessive. Proportionality analysis does not simply ask whether a different method might have been available. It asks whether the measure adopted is constitutionally defensible in light of the problem and the rights affected.

The debate is difficult because verification and inclusion are both essential. A process designed only to remove doubtful entries could exclude genuine voters through paperwork barriers. A process that never checks records could allow inaccuracies to accumulate. Fair design therefore depends on notice, accessible ways to respond, clear standards of evidence, adequate time and meaningful correction mechanisms. The administrative convenience of a central database cannot by itself justify making it impossible for a person to correct an error.

The judgment is best understood as an examination of institutional power and its limits, not as a general permission to disregard statutory safeguards. The constitutional objective of accurate rolls must be pursued through lawful methods. For students of public law, the case illustrates how the Election Commission's independence, Parliament's authority and the citizen's interest in an inclusive electoral process must be considered together.

passages.title: Biodiversity targets and the Yerevan review

sources.title: COP17: Nations chart Yerevan Pathway to speed up action for nature

passages.text:
The loss of biodiversity is not limited to the disappearance of rare animals. It includes the decline of ecosystems, the fragmentation of habitats, the loss of genetic diversity and the weakening of ecological processes on which food, water and human livelihoods depend. Because species and ecosystems cross political borders, governments have built international frameworks for cooperation. The Convention on Biological Diversity is one such treaty framework. Its Conference of the Parties, commonly called the COP, provides a forum where participating governments review implementation and negotiate collective decisions.

The seventeenth meeting of the Conference of the Parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity took place in Yerevan, Armenia, from 19 to 30 October 2026. The Convention's official conference page describes the meeting as the first global review of collective progress towards implementing the Kunming–Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework. That framework, adopted in 2022, sets a shared direction for halting and reversing biodiversity loss by 2030. A global review is important because a target that is accepted in a diplomatic document must still be translated into national plans, budgets, laws and local action.

On 1 November 2026, the United Nations reported that countries meeting in Armenia had charted a Yerevan Pathway to accelerate action for nature. The UN account said that the global review found the world off track to meet its biodiversity targets. A progress review can have two functions. It can identify areas where national action is insufficient, and it can help governments decide which practical barriers should be addressed next. It does not itself restore a wetland, reduce illegal trade or reconnect fragmented habitats. Those results depend on implementation after delegates leave the conference hall.

International biodiversity negotiations also expose a difficult question about resources. Countries may agree on the importance of conservation while disagreeing about who should pay, how funds should be distributed and how progress should be measured. Developing countries may argue that ambitious global expectations require predictable finance and access to technology. Donor governments may seek transparency and evidence that funds produce measurable benefits. Both concerns can be legitimate, but an unresolved financing debate can slow action where ecological loss is already occurring.

COP17 should not be confused with a climate conference under the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change. Biodiversity and climate are connected: forests and wetlands store carbon, while changing temperatures affect habitats. Yet the treaty processes and their negotiating questions are distinct. For a student, the key point is that the CBD addresses the conservation and sustainable use of biological diversity and the fair sharing of benefits arising from genetic resources. Its targets require national implementation, scientific monitoring and cooperation across borders.

passages.title: A change in the RBI policy rate

sources.title: Liquidity Adjustment Facility: Change in rates

passages.text:
A central bank's policy rate influences the price at which short-term funds move through the banking system. It does not mechanically determine every loan rate paid by a household or business, but it affects the broader conditions under which credit is priced. When a central bank raises its policy rate, borrowing can become more expensive over time, demand may moderate and inflationary pressure may ease. The same action can also slow investment or consumption, so the decision involves a balance between price stability and economic activity.

At its meeting held from 5 to 7 October 2026, the Reserve Bank of India's Monetary Policy Committee voted unanimously to increase the policy repo rate under the liquidity adjustment facility by 25 basis points, from 5.25 per cent to 5.50 per cent. The RBI's notification dated 7 October gave effect to the change. The Standing Deposit Facility rate was adjusted to 5.25 per cent, while the Marginal Standing Facility rate and Bank Rate became 5.75 per cent. The Committee also changed its policy stance from neutral to calibrated tightening. Two members expressed a preference for retaining a neutral stance.

The RBI's statement described a difficult global setting, including renewed conflict in West Asia and sharp volatility in crude-oil prices. An increase in energy prices can affect transport, production and household costs. If the initial price shock spreads into wages and a wider range of goods and services, inflation may become more persistent. A central bank must consider such second-round effects rather than responding only to the first movement in fuel prices. At the same time, a rate increase cannot produce more oil or repair a disrupted supply chain. Monetary policy works through demand, expectations and financial conditions, not by directly creating missing goods.

The term calibrated tightening signals a direction of policy rather than an unconditional promise to raise rates at every future meeting. The RBI indicated that later decisions would depend on actual growth and inflation developments, including whether price pressures broaden. A policy stance is therefore not the same thing as a binding schedule of future increases. It communicates how the Committee currently views the balance of risks.

The episode illustrates why central-bank communication matters. Households may hear that a rate has changed and assume that all borrowing costs will immediately move by the same amount. In reality, transmission varies by loan contract, bank funding costs, competition and timing. A clear reading of a policy announcement separates the committee's decision, the operational rates that follow, its explanation of economic conditions and its conditional guidance about future action.

passages.title: The duty to give reasons
passages.text:
Assume that a public authority has the power to grant or refuse a licence. The governing principle is that a decision affecting a person's rights or important interests must ordinarily give intelligible reasons. Reasons should identify the material facts considered, the rule applied and the link between the two. The purpose is not to require a lengthy essay for every administrative action. It is to allow the affected person to understand the decision, make a meaningful challenge where appropriate and permit a reviewing body to determine whether the authority acted within its powers.

The duty may be limited where a statute expressly provides a different procedure, but a general desire for administrative convenience is not enough to erase it. An authority may use standard forms or concise reasons, provided the explanation is specific enough to show that the case was considered rather than decided by an inflexible formula. Merely repeating the words of a rule does not explain why the person's conduct or circumstances satisfy that rule.

Consider an application for a street-food permit. The authority refuses it by stating that the application is 'not in the public interest'. That phrase may describe a legally relevant objective, but on its own it gives the applicant no clue whether the refusal concerns sanitation, pedestrian access, capacity limits or an unrelated preference. If the authority has relied on a documented obstruction at the proposed site, a short explanation identifying the obstruction and the relevant safety rule may be sufficient. If it has relied on a mistaken address, the applicant should be able to correct that factual error.

Reasons also improve decision-making inside an institution. An officer who must identify the evidence and explain the applicable rule is more likely to notice a gap in the file or a conflict between two considerations. This does not guarantee that the decision will be correct. A reasoned decision can still be unlawful, irrational or based on weak evidence. But the act of giving reasons makes the path to the outcome visible and therefore easier to test.

There may be genuine situations in which immediate interim action is necessary to prevent serious harm. In such a case, the authority may act first if the governing rule permits it, but it should record the urgent basis and provide a fuller explanation and opportunity to respond as soon as reasonably possible. Urgency should be demonstrated, not merely asserted. The exception is narrow because a temporary step can have lasting consequences.

Apply only these principles to the questions below. Do not assume that every administrative decision requires the same length of explanation, or that a short explanation is necessarily inadequate. The central test is whether the reasons, read in context, make the authority's actual basis understandable and reviewable.

passages.title: Consent and responsible data use
passages.text:
Assume the following data-protection principle for this passage. An organisation that collects personal information must tell the individual, in clear language, why the information is being collected and how it will be used. Consent is valid only when it is informed, specific and freely given. Information collected for one purpose must not automatically be used for an unrelated purpose. The organisation should collect no more information than reasonably necessary, protect what it holds and delete or anonymise it when the stated need ends, unless a lawful retention obligation applies.

A consent request hidden inside a long document may fail the clarity requirement even if a box has been ticked. A person should be able to understand the essential choice without needing specialist knowledge. Equally, a service should not treat silence as consent where the principle requires an affirmative choice. Consent must also be free: where refusing an optional use does not prevent the core service from being delivered, the organisation should not threaten to deny that service merely because the person declines the optional use.

The principle recognises that not all processing needs the same explanation or the same amount of data. A delivery service may need a customer's address to deliver a parcel, but it would be difficult to justify using that address to build an unrelated advertising profile without a separate basis and disclosure. A school may need emergency contact details to protect students, but that does not make every possible secondary use automatically acceptable. The question is whether the proposed use is reasonably connected to the stated purpose and has been explained in a way the individual can understand.

Security is a separate but related obligation. An organisation cannot avoid responsibility by saying that a breach was caused by an outside attacker if reasonable safeguards were not maintained. Appropriate protection may depend on the sensitivity and volume of information, the likely harm from disclosure and the available security measures. The principle does not demand perfect security, but it does require reasonable care.

An individual must also have a practical way to exercise the choice. A consent button that is easy to press but impossible to withdraw may undermine the claim that consent is freely given. Withdrawal does not necessarily erase a record that must lawfully be retained, but the organisation should stop the optional use for which consent was withdrawn. It should explain any limited retention that continues.

These rules are supplied for the exercise and are not a statement of every requirement in any particular statute. The questions test whether a proposed collection or use is consistent with the principles stated here, not whether the candidate can recall a separate legal provision.

passages.title: Reasonable accommodation in a public examination
passages.text:
Assume that an examination authority must provide reasonable accommodation to a candidate with a disability when the requested adjustment enables meaningful participation and does not fundamentally alter the skill being assessed or impose a disproportionate burden. The authority must examine the candidate's actual needs and the nature of the examination. It may not reject every request by applying a blanket rule. Equally, the duty does not require an authority to provide an adjustment that changes the essential nature of the assessment.

A request for additional time may be reasonable where the candidate's disability affects the speed of reading or writing but the examination is intended to test comprehension rather than speed. The authority should consider relevant evidence and whether the additional time can be administered fairly. A request to have another person select answers on the candidate's behalf may be more difficult where independent selection is the very skill being examined. The authority should distinguish between assistance that removes an irrelevant barrier and assistance that performs the assessed task.

The process matters. A candidate should be told what documents are required, how to submit them and when a decision will be made. Where a request is incomplete, the authority should ordinarily identify the missing information rather than reject it without explanation. It may ask for clarification, but it should avoid demanding material that has no real connection to the adjustment sought. A form designed for one type of disability may not capture the needs of another.

The authority may refuse a particular adjustment if reliable evidence shows that it would compromise a genuine safety requirement or fundamentally alter what the test measures. It should explain that conclusion and consider workable alternatives. A claim that providing separate seating is inconvenient, for example, is not enough by itself if the arrangement is practical and would enable participation. A claimed burden should be assessed in light of cost, available resources, frequency of the request and the importance of equal access.

Reasonable accommodation is not identical treatment. Treating every candidate in exactly the same way can preserve an existing disadvantage when the assessment environment creates a barrier unrelated to the skill being tested. At the same time, the aim is not to guarantee a particular score or outcome. The aim is to provide a fair opportunity to demonstrate the ability that the examination legitimately measures.

Apply only the principle above. The examination authority is not required to accept every requested measure, but it must engage with the request, assess the relevant evidence and explain why the proposed adjustment is or is not reasonable.

passages.title: Notice, cancellation and a fair contract
passages.text:
Assume that a consumer service contract contains a cancellation clause. The governing principle is that a business may enforce a disclosed cancellation charge only if the term was brought to the consumer's attention before the contract was concluded, the charge is proportionate to a genuine loss or administrative cost, and the consumer had a reasonable opportunity to understand the term. A term hidden in a document delivered after payment cannot ordinarily be used to create a new financial obligation. A business may still recover a legally recognised loss where the consumer has clearly agreed to the relevant term and the amount is fair.

The timing of notice is important. A hotel that displays a cancellation policy before a customer pays gives the customer an opportunity to compare options. A travel operator that sends the policy only after confirming a booking has not necessarily obtained agreement to that term. The fact that a link existed somewhere on a website does not prove that a reasonable customer was directed to it or could understand its importance.

Proportionality is not determined only by the label used by the business. Calling a charge an 'administration fee' does not make it reasonable. The business should be able to explain the work performed, the costs incurred or the loss caused by the cancellation. A fixed charge may be fair where the cost is predictable and the amount is modest. A charge equal to the entire contract price may be difficult to justify where the service can be resold and little expense has been incurred.

The consumer's conduct can matter. A person who cancels shortly before a reserved service is delivered may cause a greater loss than someone who cancels weeks in advance. A clause that varies charges according to notice period may therefore be more proportionate than one that imposes the same amount in every case. The business should also avoid double recovery: it should not recover the full price from the first customer and then charge a second customer for the same service without accounting for the benefit received.

A fair contract is not one that eliminates all risk for the consumer or all cost for the business. It allocates foreseeable risks in a way that is clear and proportionate. The principle protects informed choice while recognising that a genuine cancellation can cause real expense.

For each question, apply only the supplied rule. Do not assume that a charge is automatically invalid merely because it is inconvenient, or automatically valid merely because it appears in a document.

passages.title: Precaution and environmental decision-making
passages.text:
Assume that a public authority is considering permission for an industrial facility near a wetland. The governing principle is that where credible evidence indicates a risk of serious or irreversible environmental harm, the decision-maker must take reasonable precautionary measures even if scientific certainty is incomplete. The principle does not require an automatic ban on every activity that carries some environmental risk. It requires the authority to identify the plausible harm, examine the quality of available evidence, consider less harmful alternatives and impose safeguards proportionate to the risk.

The burden of producing information may fall more heavily on the project proponent when that proponent controls the technical data about the proposed activity. A company that knows the chemicals, quantities and waste process should not be able to rely on the absence of public data as proof that no risk exists. The authority may require a credible impact assessment, independent testing or a monitoring plan. It should also disclose the material findings so that affected communities can respond meaningfully.

Precaution is not the same as speculation. A bare assertion that any industrial activity will destroy an ecosystem is not enough. There should be a plausible pathway between the activity and the feared harm. For example, evidence that a proposed discharge could alter water quality may justify additional treatment requirements or a different discharge location. If reliable evidence shows that a particular risk can be controlled through a technically feasible measure, the authority may consider approval subject to that measure.

The principle also recognises uncertainty in the other direction. A project may promise employment or improved infrastructure, but those benefits should be assessed rather than assumed. The authority should compare alternatives, including different sites, production methods and project scales. A decision that merely lists benefits without explaining how environmental risks will be managed is incomplete. So is a decision that rejects the project without examining whether a less harmful design is possible.

Monitoring should be connected to enforceable conditions. If the authority requires water samples, it should specify who will collect them, how often, what threshold triggers action and what remedy follows a breach. A monitoring condition that has no consequence may provide little protection. The authority should also be prepared to revise permission if new evidence shows that the original assessment was materially wrong.

Apply the stated precautionary principle to the situations below. It calls for reasoned prevention and adaptive oversight, not certainty at any cost and not unexamined permission in the face of credible serious risk.

passages.title: A city debates a bus-priority lane
passages.text:
The transport department proposes a dedicated bus lane on a crowded avenue. It argues that buses carry many more passengers than private cars and that allowing buses to bypass queues will improve reliability. A business association objects that removing a general traffic lane will make deliveries slower and discourage customers from visiting shops. The department replies that smoother bus journeys may attract some commuters away from cars, reducing the number of vehicles using the avenue. Both sides identify plausible effects, but neither has yet established the overall result.

The strongest case for a bus lane depends on more than the number of people who currently ride buses. It also depends on whether the lane will materially reduce journey times, whether those savings are reliable throughout the day and whether the service has enough capacity to absorb additional passengers. If buses remain crowded or arrive irregularly, a faster lane may not persuade many drivers to switch. Conversely, if the bus service is frequent and dependable, a modest reduction in travel time may have a larger effect than the department expects.

The business association's concern also needs evidence. Some customers arrive by car, but others walk, cycle or use public transport. Deliveries may be scheduled at different times, and loading arrangements may be redesigned. A lane that reduces access for delivery vehicles at every hour could harm businesses. A scheme that provides designated loading windows and protects pedestrian access may produce a different result. The mere fact that one lane is removed does not prove that every shop will receive fewer customers.

The department proposes to compare the avenue with similar roads before and after implementation. A useful evaluation would measure bus travel time, passenger numbers, traffic on nearby streets, delivery delays and retail activity. It would also record whether the comparison roads experienced unrelated changes, such as construction or a new shopping centre. Without that control, a rise or fall in sales might be incorrectly attributed to the bus lane.

A pilot scheme can provide information, but only if the department defines success and failure in advance. If it measures only bus speed, it may overlook traffic displacement. If it measures only car delay, it may ignore the number of people moved. The right evaluation should reflect the stated public objective and monitor significant side effects.

The proposal is therefore neither proved nor disproved by the arguments currently offered. Its case will become stronger if evidence shows meaningful gains in person-throughput and reliable buses without unacceptable harm to access or surrounding streets.

passages.title: The limits of a research ranking
passages.text:
A university announces that it will distribute research grants according to a ranking based on the number of papers published by each department. The administration argues that publication counts are easy to verify and provide a consistent way to compare activity. Some faculty members object that the method rewards quantity rather than quality. They point out that a department working in a field where experiments take many years may publish fewer papers than one that produces shorter studies. The administration responds that quality is difficult to measure and that a simple count is at least objective.

The ranking does measure something: the number of publications recorded under the chosen rules. It does not, without further assumptions, measure the importance, originality or reliability of the work. A high count may reflect a large team, a field with shorter publication cycles or a practice of dividing one project into several papers. A low count may reflect a small research group or work that requires long observation. The measure is not meaningless, but it is narrower than the claim that it measures research excellence.

Replacing publication count with citation count would not automatically solve the problem. Citations vary by discipline and may reflect criticism as well as approval. Highly specialised research may be valuable while being read by a small audience. Peer review can provide expert judgement but may reproduce institutional bias or favour familiar methods. Each metric captures one dimension and creates incentives that researchers may learn to optimise.

The university could use several indicators and require departments to explain their research plans. It might consider peer assessment, data quality, public impact, student involvement and field-specific time frames. A mixed method would be more complex and could involve subjective judgement, so safeguards would be needed to explain how decisions are made and to allow correction of factual errors. Complexity is not necessarily unfair, just as simplicity is not necessarily neutral.

The central question is what the grant programme is intended to support. If the purpose is to reward current publication volume, a count may be suitable. If the purpose is to fund promising work that may produce important results over several years, a count alone is poorly matched to the objective. The choice of metric should follow the purpose rather than determine it.

A ranking becomes misleading when its users forget the limits of the measure. The solution is not always to abandon numbers, but to state what they can show, what they cannot show and how other evidence will be considered.

passages.title: Remote work and the measurement problem
passages.text:
A company reports that employees who work from the office complete more tasks each week than employees who work remotely. Management concludes that office attendance causes higher productivity and proposes a mandatory five-day office policy. Employees challenge the inference. They point out that senior staff, whose work may involve fewer but more complex tasks, are more likely to work remotely, while employees in routine roles attend the office more often. The reported difference may therefore reflect job composition rather than location.

The comparison is also incomplete if it counts tasks without measuring their difficulty, accuracy or value. A person who resolves a difficult client problem may complete fewer tasks than someone processing a large number of standard requests. If the company rewards raw task counts, employees may choose simpler work or divide a single task into several entries. A useful productivity measure should reflect the purpose of the role and the quality of the outcome.

Even if the data were adjusted for job type, the company would need to consider selection effects. Employees who prefer office work may choose roles that require in-person collaboration. Those who work remotely may have more experience or may be assigned projects that are harder to measure. A comparison of existing groups cannot automatically show what would happen if the same employees changed location. The company needs evidence that helps isolate the effect of location from these other factors.

A pilot could assign comparable teams to different work arrangements for a defined period, while keeping tasks, staffing and performance measures as similar as practical. The pilot should record output quality, deadlines, staff retention, commuting burdens, collaboration and customer feedback. It should also allow for the possibility that different roles need different arrangements. A uniform rule may be easier to administer, but administrative simplicity alone does not show that it produces better results.

The argument for office attendance may still be supported by evidence about mentoring, trust, security or rapid coordination. Those benefits should be stated directly rather than inferred from a task-count comparison. Similarly, remote work should not be assumed to improve satisfaction or productivity for every employee. The relevant question is not which arrangement is ideologically preferable, but which arrangement best supports the organisation's objectives for particular kinds of work.

A credible decision should identify the outcome it seeks, compare like with like and consider costs that are not visible in a weekly task report. Until that evidence is available, the company's causal conclusion is premature.

passages.title: Water conservation and household behaviour
passages.text:
A municipal council observes that households in districts receiving free water-saving devices use less water on average than households in districts that did not receive them. It concludes that the devices caused the reduction and proposes distributing them across the city. A review group agrees that the result is promising but asks whether the two sets of districts were comparable before the programme began. The device districts may have experienced stricter restrictions, different rainfall or a change in the number of residents.

The council's evidence may show an association, but a causal conclusion requires attention to alternative explanations. If water use was already lower in the districts selected for the programme, the device may deserve less credit. If a drought warning was issued at the same time, households may have reduced use regardless of the equipment. A stronger evaluation would compare changes over time between similar districts and record relevant differences in weather, occupancy and enforcement.

The group also questions the use of an average. A city-wide mean may fall even if a small number of high-use properties account for most of the reduction. That might still be useful, but it would not show whether ordinary households changed behaviour or whether the programme reached areas where scarcity is most severe. Distributional information can reveal who benefited and who continues to face high water costs.

There is also a distinction between efficiency and conservation. A device may reduce the volume needed for a particular activity, such as flushing or washing, but households may respond by using the saved water elsewhere. This rebound effect does not make the device useless; it means that technical efficiency may not translate one-for-one into lower total consumption. Clear information, leak repairs and fair pricing may complement equipment distribution.

The council can still proceed with a wider programme if the devices are low-cost and the expected benefit is credible. But the decision should be described as a policy trial or an evidence-informed expansion rather than proof that every household will reduce use by the same amount. Monitoring should track actual consumption and ensure that low-income households are not penalised for conditions they cannot control, such as leaking shared pipes.

The argument is strongest when it separates the observed result from the explanation offered for it. A reduction has been recorded. The cause, scale and durability of that reduction require further testing.

options.text: The choice may not be freely given because an optional use is made a condition of the core service.
The organisation is required to provide unrelated services.
The person has consented by visiting the website.
The organisation must delete every record immediately.

questions.explanation: The passage says optional processing should not be forced when the core service can be delivered without it.

questions.prompt: Which practice best satisfies data minimisation?

options.text: Collect every available data field in case it may become useful.
Collect only information reasonably necessary for the stated service purpose.
Ask for sensitive information even when it has no connection to the service.
Retain all information permanently without review.

questions.explanation: The principle expressly requires collecting no more than reasonably necessary.

questions.prompt: A company suffers a breach after failing to install reasonable safeguards. Which statement follows?

options.text: The company is exempt whenever an outsider is involved.
Any cyberattack automatically proves compliance.
It cannot avoid responsibility merely by pointing to the attacker.
A breach means consent was never required.

questions.explanation: The passage states that reasonable protection remains an organisational obligation.

questions.prompt: After withdrawal of consent for optional advertising, what should the organisation ordinarily do?

options.text: Continue advertising because consent was once given.
Treat withdrawal as consent to a different use.
Delete every record regardless of legal retention duties.
Stop the optional use while retaining only information that must lawfully be kept.

questions.explanation: The passage distinguishes stopping optional processing from lawful limited retention.

questions.prompt: An exam tests reading comprehension, but a candidate with a documented disability requests additional time because reading speed is affected. What is the best approach?

options.text: Assess whether extra time removes an irrelevant barrier without changing the skill being tested.
Grant any amount requested without considering the exam's purpose.
Reject the request automatically because all candidates must receive identical time.
Require the candidate to choose answers through another person.

questions.explanation: The passage requires an individual assessment tied to meaningful participation and the skill assessed.

questions.prompt: A candidate requests that another person select the answers in a test designed to measure independent comprehension. What concern is strongest?

options.text: The request must be granted because it is inexpensive.
The assistance may perform the very skill that the examination is intended to assess.
The authority must guarantee the candidate a passing score.
Any assistance is prohibited in every examination.

questions.explanation: The principle distinguishes barrier removal from assistance that changes the essential assessed task.

questions.prompt: The authority rejects a request because a form is incomplete but does not identify what is missing. Which principle is most relevant?

options.text: The candidate should ordinarily be told what information is missing and allowed to clarify.
The authority can disregard the request without reading it.
A candidate must always provide unrelated medical records.
An incomplete form must be accepted without any review.

questions.explanation: The passage describes a fair process requiring clear requirements and a chance to supply relevant information.

questions.prompt: Which reason could justify refusing a particular adjustment under the supplied rule?

options.text: A general preference for treating everyone identically.
Reliable evidence that it would fundamentally alter the skill being assessed.
A desire to reduce administrative correspondence.
A claim that separate seating is inconvenient without further evidence.

questions.explanation: A refusal can be justified where the adjustment changes the essential nature of the test or creates disproportionate burden.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of reasonable accommodation as described?

options.text: To remove all assessment standards for selected candidates.
To ensure every candidate obtains the same score.
To guarantee identical arrangements regardless of individual needs.
To provide a fair opportunity to demonstrate the ability the examination legitimately measures.

questions.explanation: The passage explicitly distinguishes fair opportunity from a guaranteed outcome.

questions.prompt: An authority can provide a requested adjustment at modest cost without affecting test integrity. What follows?

options.text: It may ignore the candidate's actual circumstances.
It must demand proof unrelated to the request.
It should ordinarily provide it if it enables meaningful participation.
It may refuse simply because the adjustment is not available to every candidate.

questions.explanation: The stated principle requires reasonable adjustments unless they alter the task or impose disproportionate burden.

questions.prompt: A cancellation fee appears only in a document sent after a customer pays. Under the passage, what is the strongest objection?

options.text: The term was not brought to the customer's attention before the contract was concluded.
The customer can never be charged for a late cancellation.
Every cancellation fee is prohibited.
A business must always refund the full price regardless of loss.

questions.explanation: The principle makes timely disclosure a condition for enforcing the agreed cancellation term.

questions.prompt: A business calls a charge an 'administration fee' but cannot explain any cost or loss. What follows?

options.text: The consumer must pay any fee stated by a business.
The amount is automatically a tax.
The charge becomes valid because the label is neutral.
The label alone does not establish that the charge is proportionate.

questions.explanation: The passage says the business must explain the cost or loss; terminology cannot replace evidence.

questions.prompt: Why might a cancellation scale based on notice period be fairer than a fixed charge?

options.text: It prevents a consumer from cancelling at any time.
It can reflect the different losses caused by early and late cancellation.
It guarantees that the business earns a profit on every booking.
It removes the need to disclose the contract term.

questions.explanation: The passage notes that late cancellation may cause greater loss than cancellation weeks earlier.

questions.prompt: A hotel can resell a cancelled room but still charges the entire original price without accounting for the resale. Which concern arises?

options.text: The cancellation clause automatically becomes a criminal offence.
The hotel is required to pay the customer twice.
The hotel may be recovering more than its genuine loss.
The consumer has no right to notice.

questions.explanation: The passage warns against double recovery and disproportionate charges.

questions.prompt: Which fact most strongly supports enforceability of a cancellation term under the supplied rule?

options.text: It imposes the full price regardless of timing or loss.
It was clearly disclosed before payment and imposes a proportionate charge linked to genuine cost.
It was described only verbally after the service date.
It was hidden in a link shown after booking.

questions.explanation: The stated principle requires advance disclosure, proportionality and a reasonable opportunity to understand.

questions.prompt: What balance does the passage seek to achieve?

options.text: Protect informed consumer choice while recognising genuine business costs.
Eliminate every financial risk for businesses.
Remove contractual freedom from both parties.
Ensure consumers pay every amount requested.

questions.explanation: The final paragraph states that a fair contract allocates foreseeable risks clearly and proportionately.

questions.prompt: A proposed factory has credible evidence linking its discharge to serious wetland damage, but the exact scale is uncertain. What does the principle require?

options.text: Ignoring the evidence until damage becomes visible.
Automatic approval because the harm is not certain.
Reasonable precautionary measures and further assessment before permission is granted.
Automatic refusal of every industrial project near water.

questions.explanation: The principle requires precaution where credible evidence indicates serious or irreversible harm despite incomplete certainty.

questions.prompt: Why may the project proponent be required to produce technical information?

options.text: It is automatically guilty of causing harm.
The authority has no responsibility to assess evidence.
Only the proponent can decide what the public may know.
It controls much of the data about the activity and its likely effects.

questions.explanation: The passage says the party controlling relevant technical data should not rely on public ignorance as proof of safety.

questions.prompt: Which proposal best illustrates precaution rather than speculation?

options.text: Reject the project solely because a resident dislikes factories.
Require independent testing where evidence indicates that a specific discharge may alter water quality.
Approve the project because the company promises jobs.
Ban every activity that involves machinery without examining its effects.

questions.explanation: Precaution requires a plausible pathway between the activity and a serious harm, supported by evidence.

questions.prompt: An authority approves a project but requires samples with no threshold, responsible tester or consequence for breach. What is the weakness?

options.text: Any sample requirement automatically prevents harm.
Monitoring is never relevant after approval.
The company is exempt from all other conditions.
The monitoring condition may be ineffective because it is not connected to enforceable action.

questions.explanation: The passage says monitoring needs clear responsibility, frequency, thresholds and remedies.

questions.prompt: Which consideration should form part of a reasoned environmental decision?

options.text: Whether a less harmful site, method or project scale is feasible.
Only the authority's administrative convenience.
Whether the company has used an attractive project name.
Only the number of jobs promised by the proponent.

questions.explanation: The principle requires examination of alternatives and comparison of environmental risk and public benefit.

questions.prompt: What is the best description of the precautionary principle in the passage?

options.text: A presumption that economic benefits always override environmental harm.
A rule requiring certainty before any action is taken.
Reasoned prevention and adaptive oversight where credible serious risk exists.
A blanket prohibition on all activity with any possible risk.

questions.explanation: The final paragraph states that precaution is neither certainty at any cost nor unexamined permission.

questions.prompt: What is the transport department's main conclusion?

options.text: The bus lane will eliminate all traffic congestion.
Every shop will receive more customers immediately.
Delivery vehicles should be prohibited from the avenue.
A dedicated bus lane can improve bus reliability and attract some commuters from cars.

questions.explanation: The department argues that faster and more reliable buses may reduce car use and improve person movement.

questions.prompt: Which assumption is most important to the department's argument?

options.text: The avenue has no delivery traffic.
The bus lane will improve bus journeys enough to influence travel choices.
Retail activity is unrelated to transport access.
Every current driver already prefers public transport.

questions.explanation: Without a meaningful improvement in bus service, the predicted shift from cars is less plausible.

questions.prompt: Which evidence would most strengthen the department's case?

options.text: A pilot shows faster, more reliable buses and increased passenger numbers without major traffic displacement.
A business association repeats its concern about delivery delays.
A report counts the number of buses owned by the city.
A survey shows that some residents dislike buses.

questions.explanation: The pilot would support both the mechanism and the outcome predicted by the department.

questions.prompt: Which fact would most weaken the claim that the lane reduces congestion overall?

options.text: Some commuters switch from cars to buses.
The lane operates during peak travel hours.
Traffic diverted to nearby streets increases total delay and safety risks across the area.
Bus passengers report improved reliability.

questions.explanation: The wider-area effects could offset gains on the avenue and undermine the overall claim.

questions.prompt: Why does the passage recommend comparing similar roads before and after the pilot?

options.text: To ensure that every road has identical traffic volumes.
To prove that the pilot is popular.
To avoid measuring bus travel times.
To help distinguish the bus-lane effect from unrelated changes occurring at the same time.

questions.explanation: A comparison can help control for outside changes such as construction or new developments.

questions.prompt: Which evaluation would be incomplete if used alone?

options.text: Measuring only bus speed while ignoring traffic displacement and access effects.
Recording both delivery access and person-throughput.
Reviewing passenger numbers and reliability after a defined pilot.
Measuring bus speed, passenger numbers and nearby-street traffic together.

questions.explanation: A single metric can miss important side effects and the public objective's wider dimensions.

questions.prompt: What does the publication-count ranking directly measure?

options.text: The originality of every research project.
The reliability of all findings.
The number of publications recorded under the chosen rules.
The long-term social value of each department's work.

questions.explanation: The passage accepts that the metric measures publication volume but not broader quality by itself.

questions.prompt: Which assumption underlies the administration's use of publication counts?

options.text: Every discipline has identical publication cycles.
Publication volume is a sufficiently useful proxy for the grant programme's objective.
Research quality can never be assessed by experts.
Every paper receives the same number of citations.

questions.explanation: The administration relies on the count as a consistent comparison of research activity.

questions.prompt: Which example best illustrates why raw counts may be unfair?

options.text: A researcher submits work to peer review.
Every department uses the same reporting period.
A publication is checked for factual accuracy.
A field requiring years of observation produces fewer papers than a field with short study cycles.

questions.explanation: Different research timelines can affect output counts independently of quality.

questions.prompt: Why would replacing publication count with citation count not automatically solve the problem?

options.text: Citation counts are never measurable.
Citation patterns vary by discipline and may reflect criticism as well as approval.
Citations are assigned only by university administrators.
A paper cannot be cited more than once.

questions.explanation: The passage identifies limits of citations as another imperfect metric.

questions.prompt: Which additional measure would best complement publication count?

options.text: The colour of a department's annual report.
The number of offices allocated to each professor.
Peer assessment combined with field-sensitive evidence about quality and impact.
The age of the university's oldest building.

questions.explanation: A mixed method can capture dimensions that raw counts omit, with safeguards against bias.

questions.prompt: What is the central warning about rankings?

options.text: A metric becomes misleading when users forget the limited thing it measures.
All numerical evaluation should be abandoned.
Research should be funded without any stated purpose.
Simple indicators are always more reliable than complex ones.

questions.explanation: The passage concludes that users must state what a measure does and does not show.

questions.prompt: What flaw affects the company's conclusion about office attendance?

options.text: It compares the same workers under identical conditions.
It assumes that employees perform any tasks at all.
It measures too many different employee groups.
It infers causation from a comparison that may reflect differences in job roles.

questions.explanation: The passage identifies job composition as a possible confounding factor.

questions.prompt: Which alternative explanation does the employee group provide?

options.text: Office-based staff have no performance targets.
Senior staff doing complex work are more likely to work remotely.
All roles produce identical numbers of tasks.
Remote staff are always new employees.

questions.explanation: This role difference could explain the reported task-count gap without a location effect.

questions.prompt: Which measure would best improve the company's productivity comparison?

options.text: Treat every task as equally valuable without checking.
Count only the number of entries in the task system.
Assess output quality and task difficulty alongside task counts.
Exclude difficult projects from the records.

questions.explanation: The passage argues that quantity alone may reward simple or artificially divided tasks.

questions.prompt: Which design would provide stronger evidence about location effects?

options.text: A pilot using comparable teams and consistent measures across different work arrangements.
A survey asking only the most satisfied employees.
A comparison of unrelated departments with different workloads.
A count of office access-card swipes.

questions.explanation: A controlled pilot can reduce differences in task, staffing and measurement.

questions.prompt: Which inference is supported about a five-day office rule?

options.text: Office attendance necessarily reduces productivity.
The company has no legitimate interest in collaboration.
Administrative uniformity does not itself establish that the rule improves performance.
All roles should permanently remain remote.

questions.explanation: The passage says a uniform rule may be simpler but needs evidence that it serves organisational objectives.

questions.prompt: Which evidence would most weaken management's causal claim?

options.text: Remote employees have a longer commute.
After adjusting for role and task difficulty, the productivity difference disappears.
The company buys new office furniture.
A few employees say they like the office.

questions.explanation: If the observed difference disappears after controlling for role, location is less likely to be the cause.

questions.prompt: What has the council directly observed?

options.text: The devices alone caused the entire reduction.
Every household reduced use by the same amount.
City-wide consumption has permanently fallen.
Districts receiving water-saving devices used less water on average than comparison districts.

questions.explanation: The passage carefully states the observed association without claiming its cause.

questions.prompt: Which alternative factor could explain part of the reduction?

options.text: A drought warning issued at the same time as the programme.
The districts had identical weather and occupancy.
The devices were distributed after consumption was measured.
The council measured water use in both groups.

questions.explanation: A concurrent drought warning could change behaviour independently of the devices.

questions.prompt: Why might an average conceal an important distributional effect?

options.text: An average cannot be calculated from water data.
A small number of high-use properties could account for most of the change.
An average always identifies each household's consumption.
Every household necessarily uses exactly the mean amount.

questions.explanation: The passage warns that the mean may hide differences between households and areas.

questions.prompt: What is a rebound effect in the context of this passage?

options.text: A device causes water to flow back into the reservoir.
The council refunds the cost of a water-saving device.
Households may use some of the water saved through more efficient devices for other activities.
Households stop using water entirely after installation.

questions.explanation: The passage distinguishes technical efficiency from a one-for-one fall in total consumption.

questions.prompt: Which evidence would best strengthen the causal claim?

options.text: Comparable districts show a larger reduction after installation after adjusting for weather and occupancy.
The council publishes more photographs of the devices.
Residents say they have heard of the programme.
The programme receives a national award.

questions.explanation: A controlled comparison that accounts for alternative factors would better isolate the device effect.

questions.prompt: Which conclusion is most justified by the evidence described?

options.text: The council should stop measuring consumption.
The devices are proven to reduce every household's use equally.
The programme has no value because the study is incomplete.
The programme is promising, but its causal effect and durability require further testing.

questions.explanation: The passage supports cautious expansion or further evaluation rather than an absolute claim.
